concept.title: From a physics law to a running simulation
concept.intro: Every problem in Tensorizer follows the same 1 + 7 steps: tests first (step 0), then seven steps from picture to plot. Here they are for the simplest one: a pendulum swinging under gravity. Each step matches a file you can open, run and edit in the Problems tab.
concept.s0.title: Step 0: write the tests first
concept.s0.p1: Before any solver code, write down how you will know the answer is right. In `test.py` each test is a physical law the pendulum must obey: for a tiny swing the period is $2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$, the energy $\tfrac12 mL^2\dot\theta^2 + mgL(1-\cos\theta)$ stays constant, and a big swing is slower, exactly as the elliptic integral says.
concept.s0.p2: This is test-driven development (TDD): the tests fail at first, and you write steps 4–6 until they pass. The app runs `test.py` after every render and shows a green or red TDD light. It is recommended, not enforced, and it keeps an AI agent honest too: a change that breaks the physics turns the light red.
concept.s1.title: Start from the physical picture
concept.s1.p1: A point mass $m$ hangs on a light rod of length $L$. Gravity $g$ pulls it down; the only coordinate that matters is the angle $\theta$ from the vertical.
concept.s1.p2: Decide what you want to know before writing any equation: how does $\theta$ change in time, and does a big swing take longer than a small one?
concept.s2.title: Write the law in vector form
concept.s2.p1: Newton's second law along the arc of the swing, $m L\ddot\theta = -mg\sin\theta$, gives the equation of motion:
concept.s2.p2: It is nonlinear because of $\sin\theta$, so there is no simple formula for $\theta(t)$ — a computer will march it forward in time instead. For small swings $\sin\theta\approx\theta$ and the familiar solution $\theta_0\cos(\sqrt{g/L}\,t)$ comes back.
concept.s3.title: Rewrite it in index (tensor) form
concept.s3.p1: Instead of one pendulum, release $B$ of them from different angles and give each an index $b$. The law becomes one statement about a whole tensor of angles:
concept.s3.p2: Read the indices like a spreadsheet: $\theta_b$ is a column of $B$ numbers. Nothing is summed here — each pendulum obeys the same law independently. In other problems a repeated index is summed (Einstein convention), e.g. $v_j v_j = \lvert v\rvert^2$, and that sum becomes one `torch.einsum` call.
concept.s4.title: Turn the quantities into tensors
concept.s4.p1: The state of every pendulum is its angle and angular velocity, so the whole system is one tensor $y$ of shape $(B, 2)$. A second-order equation becomes two first-order ones: $\dot\theta_b = \omega_b$ and $\dot\omega_b = -(g/L)\sin\theta_b$.
concept.s5.title: Write the law as a function
concept.s5.p1: `equation.py` is the translation step: each line of the index form becomes a line of PyTorch, applied to all pendulums at once. Comments carry the shapes so you can check them like units.
concept.s5.p2: The small-angle solution is an outer product — two indices, nothing summed — so it is written with einsum as `t,b->tb`:
concept.s6.title: Solve: march forward in time
concept.s6.p1: Fourth-order Runge–Kutta takes small steps $\Delta t$: it samples the right-hand side four times per step and combines them, with an error that shrinks like $\Delta t^4$. Because the state is a tensor, one RK4 step updates all $B$ pendulums together — on a GPU this is how thousands of simulations run in parallel.
concept.s7.title: Look at the result — and check it
concept.s7.p1: `plot.py` turns the trajectory tensor of shape $(T, B, 2)$ into an animation: each pendulum swings next to its dashed small-angle partner, and the big swings visibly fall behind.
concept.s7.p2: Never trust a simulation you have not checked. The tests compare against things we know exactly: energy $\tfrac12L^2\omega^2 + gL(1-\cos\theta)$ must stay constant, small swings must have period $2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$, and large swings must match the elliptic-integral formula.
concept.turn.title: Your turn
concept.turn.text: Open the pendulum, change the largest amplitude or gravity, tick Verbose output to watch every tensor shape go by, or edit `equation.py` — try replacing `sin(theta)` with `theta` and see the pendulums stay in step.
concept.missing: The pendulum problem is not in the library.
skills.title: The PyTorch toolbox behind every problem
skills.intro: The whole library is built from a handful of techniques. Learn them once and every problem becomes readable. Each card links to problems where you can see the technique in context and run it.
skills.tdd.title: Test first (TDD): physics as tests
skills.tdd.text: Step 0 of every problem is `test.py`: before writing the solver, state what any correct answer must satisfy, as a physical law: energy or momentum conserved, a limiting case that matches a known formula, a symmetry, or bounds such as $0 \le p \le 1$. Then write the code until the tests pass. The app runs `test.py` after every render and shows a green or red TDD light. It is recommended, not enforced, and it is also the best guard-rail for an AI agent: a change that breaks physics turns the light red.
skills.tensors.title: Tensors, shapes and devices
skills.tensors.text: Every physical quantity is a tensor with a shape you can say out loud: $B$ pendulums × 2 state variables is `(B, 2)`. Keep shapes in comments like units, and create tensors on one `device` so the same code runs on CPU or GPU.
skills.broadcasting.title: Broadcasting
skills.broadcasting.text: Combine tensors of different shapes without loops: a column `(A, 1)` against a row `(1, L)` fills an `(A, L)` table. Pairwise separations $r_{ab} = x_b - x_a$ of $N$ bodies are one subtraction.
skills.einsum.title: einsum = index notation
skills.einsum.text: `torch.einsum` is the Einstein convention typed out: name each index, repeated indices are summed. $v_j v_j$ is `'bj,bj->b'`, a matrix acting on vectors $M_{ij}y_j$ is `'ij,rj->ri'`, a cross product $\varepsilon_{ijk}v_jB_k$ uses the Levi-Civita tensor.
skills.batching.title: Batching many simulations
skills.batching.text: Add a batch index instead of a Python loop: launch angles, amplitudes, isotopes or receptor variants become one more axis, and every operation handles them together. On a GPU this is where the speed comes from.
skills.rk4.title: Time stepping (RK4)
skills.rk4.text: Write the law as $\dot y = f(y, t)$ and march forward. Classical Runge–Kutta samples $f$ four times per step with error $\propto \Delta t^4$; because $y$ is a tensor, one step updates the whole system.
skills.linalg.title: Linear algebra: solve and eigh
skills.linalg.text: Many problems are a matrix equation once discretised: $L_{ij}\phi_j = -\rho_i$ is `torch.linalg.solve`, and normal modes or quantum levels $H_{ij}\psi_j = E\,\psi_i$ come from `torch.linalg.eigh`.
skills.stencils.title: Finite differences, stencils and conv2d
skills.stencils.text: A derivative on a grid is a small stencil; the Laplacian $\partial_i\partial_i u$ is the kernel $[[0,1,0],[1,-4,1],[0,1,0]]/h^2$. `conv2d` applies it everywhere at once, and the time step must respect the CFL condition.
skills.fft.title: Spectral methods with FFT
skills.fft.text: In Fourier space a derivative is a multiplication by $ik$. Free evolution, dispersion and the kinetic step of the Schrödinger equation become element-wise products between two FFTs.
skills.autograd.title: Autograd for physics
skills.autograd.text: PyTorch can differentiate any code: forces from a potential, the mass matrix of a Lagrangian, a tidal tensor $-\partial_i\partial_j\Phi$, or Christoffel symbols from a metric $g_{\mu\nu}$ — no derivatives by hand.
skills.complex.title: Complex tensors and quantum states
skills.complex.text: Wavefunctions and fields are complex: use `torch.complex128`, `.conj()` and phases $e^{-iE_nt}$. Multi-qubit states are tensors $\psi_{ab}$, and gates act on them with einsum.
flow.title: Tensor dataflow: how the computer actually runs it
flow.intro: The first tab turns a law into tensor code. This one opens the box: what a tensor is in memory, why one line of `einsum` beats a Python loop, what a GPU does differently, and how frameworks record the computation as a dataflow graph to differentiate and speed it up. The ideas are the same in PyTorch, JAX, MLX and TensorFlow; we show PyTorch and a table of the others.
flow.name: Why “dataflow”? Tensors flow through a graph of operations: each node is a kernel, each edge a tensor. That picture, not any one library, is what the rest of this page explains.
flow.s1.title: A tensor is a block of memory with a shape
flow.s1.p1: A tensor is one flat buffer of numbers plus a little metadata: its **dtype** (for example float32, 4 bytes each), its **shape** and its **strides**, the step in memory to the next element along each axis. Element $x_{ij}$ of a $(2, 3)$ tensor sits at offset $3i + j$, so the strides are $(3, 1)$.
flow.s1.p2: Many operations only change the metadata. A transpose swaps the strides to $(1, 3)$; a slice moves the start offset and can change the shape and strides (`x[:, ::2]` doubles the column stride); none of these copies a number. Advanced indexing with a list or a mask (`x[[0, 1, 1]]`) does copy. The **device** says where the buffer lives: CPU memory or GPU memory. Step through the lab below and watch which memory cell each element reads.
flow.s1.p3: Zero-copy has a cost later. A non-contiguous tensor is read in jumps through memory, which breaks cache-line locality on the CPU and the GPU: each cache line fetched brings neighbours the next step doesn't use. When a kernel needs a contiguous buffer, `.contiguous()` is the moment the real copy happens.
flow.s2.title: Vectorise: one kernel instead of a loop
flow.s2.p1: A Python loop pays interpreter overhead for every element. A tensor operation hands the whole buffer to compiled **kernels**, which stream through memory with SIMD instructions (several numbers per CPU instruction) and many threads. One expression is not always one kernel: `a * b + c` may launch one kernel per operation, each reading and writing memory (section 6 shows how fusion merges them). Batching all cases into one tensor still pays: a few kernel launches instead of a loop over every element.
flow.s2.p2: **Broadcasting** is free in memory: `expand` gives a missing axis stride $0$, so the same numbers are reused instead of copied. `x[:, None, :] - x[None, :, :]` builds all $N^2$ pair separations as a $(N, N, 3)$ result from an $(N, 3)$ input.
flow.mem.title: Broadcasting saves the inputs, not the output
flow.mem.p1: The views `x[None, :, :]` and `x[:, None, :]` copy nothing, but the result $D_{abi} = X_{bi} - X_{ai}$ is a new tensor of $N \times N \times 3$ numbers: $12 N^2$ bytes in float32. That is 12 MB for a thousand particles, 1.2 GB for ten thousand and 120 GB for a hundred thousand, before any intermediate results or gradients. Slide $N$ below.
flow.mem.p2: So vectorisation is not about building the biggest tensor. Large problems process the pairs in chunks, keep only near neighbours (neighbour lists, sparse tensors) or use a fused kernel that never stores $D$ at all. The aim is a data layout and a sequence of operations that fit the hardware's memory.
flow.s3.title: What a GPU does differently
flow.s3.p1: A GPU runs thousands of lightweight threads at once, each handling a few elements of the same kernel, and its memory is several times faster than CPU memory. Big element-wise operations and matrix products on large batches are where it wins.
flow.s3.p2: It has fixed costs too. Launching a kernel takes microseconds, so a time loop of thousands of tiny steps on a few numbers can be faster on the CPU. Copying between CPU and GPU memory is slow: create tensors on the device once and keep them there. GPU work is asynchronous, so call `torch.cuda.synchronize()` before timing.
flow.s4.title: Contractions become matrix products
flow.s4.p1: `einsum` states a tensor contraction declaratively: which indices are summed and which are kept. Depending on the contraction pattern, the shapes and strides and the backend, it may be lowered to an optimised matrix multiplication (GEMM), a batched matrix multiplication or other kernels. Writing the index form as `einsum` keeps the mathematics exact and leaves that choice to the library; it does not promise the fastest kernel.
flow.s4.p2: Precision is a numerical modelling decision, not merely a hardware setting. float64 has about 16 significant digits, float32 about 7. Many consumer GPUs have far lower float64 than float32 throughput (data-centre GPUs much less so, and real speed also depends on memory traffic), and Apple's MPS has no float64 at all. Long time integrations, ill-conditioned matrices and cancellation can need float64 where float32 looks fine at first; Tensorizer's conservation tests are one way to find out.
flow.s5.title: The dataflow graph: gradients and speed
flow.s5.p1: While a computation runs, the framework records each operation and its inputs: a **dataflow graph** from parameters to result. Reverse-mode automatic differentiation walks the graph backwards applying the chain rule and gives the gradient of one number with respect to every input, typically for a small constant multiple of the forward cost; it has to keep intermediate results for the backward pass, so memory is often the real limit. That is how the Lagrangian, PINN and inverse-design problems get forces and gradients without writing derivatives.
flow.s5.p2: The same graph can be **compiled**: neighbouring element-wise operations are fused into one kernel so intermediate results never touch memory. PyTorch does it with `torch.compile`, JAX with `jit` (XLA), TensorFlow with `tf.function`; MLX is lazy and builds the graph until a value is needed. Eager code is easier to read and debug; compiled code is faster for long runs.
flow.s5.p3: Fusion pays because modern chips compute far faster (FLOPs) than they move data (memory bandwidth). For $A + B \times C$ the bottleneck is usually not the multiply-add but carrying the numbers from GPU memory into registers. Fusion keeps the data in registers for every operation and **writes the result back to memory only once**.
flow.s5.p4: Autograd differentiates exactly what you wrote, nothing more. In the code below $\phi = -GM/r$ is the potential per unit mass, so $-\nabla\phi$ is an acceleration; the force on a mass $m$ comes from the potential energy $U = -GMm/r$ as $\mathbf F = -\nabla U$. Naming the physical quantity correctly is still the physicist's job.
flow.s6.title: Same ideas, different frameworks
flow.s6.p1: The vocabulary changes, the principles don't. Writing the law in index notation keeps a problem portable: the `einsum` string is identical everywhere.
flow.s7.title: What Tensorizer does with all this
flow.s7.p1: Every problem builds its tensors once on `device()` (CUDA, MPS or CPU, chosen in the Backend panel), batches many cases along one axis, writes the physics as `einsum` and broadcasting, and uses float64 where a conservation law must hold to many digits. Small problems run well on a laptop CPU; the batched ones scale to a GPU unchanged.
lab.memCaption: Blue: float32, dashed violet: float64, red lines: common GPU memory sizes. Intermediates and gradients come on top.
lab.note0: x owns a new buffer of 6 float32 numbers (24 bytes). Reading row by row walks the storage in order.
lab.note1: The transpose is a view: the same 6 numbers, strides swapped. Reading it row by row jumps through storage, which is bad for cache lines.
lab.note2: A slice with a step is also a view: the column stride becomes 2, every other number is skipped.
lab.note3: None (unsqueeze) adds an axis of length 1. Still a view, still 0 new bytes.
lab.note4: expand gives the new axis stride 0: 24 logical elements read the same 6 stored numbers, each four times.
lab.note5: .contiguous() is where the copy happens: a new buffer, laid out in the transposed order.
lab.note6: einsum('ij->i') sums over j: a new tensor with one number per row.
lab.note7: einsum('ij,kj->ik') contracts j between x and x: the backend may run it as a matrix multiplication.
